s-fg2-high-0.essay:
Ottilie Brandvold knows her apprentices are young, and young binders tend to judge a book by its gold spine. On her last afternoon she doesn't just tell them patience matters. She first admits their suspicion that patience is only slowness, then proves otherwise with a story, and finally redefines repair so the hidden hours become a form of respect for the people who own the books. What makes the speech persuasive is that Brandvold practices the same quiet restraint she asks of them, ending not with a grand farewell but with an order to get back to work.

She begins by lowering expectations for her own speech: "You will not remember most of what I say this afternoon," and she admits she forgot her own teacher's speech too. This is a strange way to open a farewell, but it works on apprentices because it moves the lesson out of words and into their hands, which is where they actually spend all day. Lifting a torn signature "the way you would lift a sleeping child from a chair" turns technical skill into tenderness, and sets up the idea that what matters is what they do "when nobody is watching."

Next she gives them numbers. Of every ten hours, "perhaps one produces something a reader can see." For apprentices who measure their work by gold and marbled endpapers, this is a correction, the part they are proud of is a tenth of the job. She lists the other nine hours, sewing, paring leather "to the thickness of a petal," pressing, waiting, then warns that a hinge glued too soon "will split in the hands of a stranger three years from now, in a town you will never visit." The cause and effect gives invisible work visible consequences, just delayed and far away. Then the sentences shrink: "Nobody will thank you for the nine hours. Do them anyway." After the long list, the short command lands like a verdict.

Brandvold seems to know this won't convince everyone, so she voices their doubt herself: "Patience is a pretty word old people use to excuse slowness." Instead of brushing it aside she partly agrees, describing a patience that is "only fear wearing an apron." The concession makes her sound honest rather than nostalgic, and it lets her sharpen her own definition by contrast. Her patience "is not the absence of hurry. It is the refusal of it." The antithesis turns patience from something passive, which a young person finds boring, into an act of will, which sounds almost brave.

Having made the claim, she supplies proof with Mrs. Alder's hymnal. She leaves the stain under the kitchen tape "because that stain was the child," and Mrs. Alder weeps "Not because I had failed to hide it. Because I had not tried." The apprentices' objection gets answered in a way they wouldn't expect: the eleven days were not slowness, they were what it took to keep the book's history intact. This leads straight into her definition, where replacement says "here is another" but repair says "it is still itself." By adding "Any factory can replace," she gives them a reason to be proud of slow work, since it's the one thing a machine can't do.

The ending is where the speech does what it says. Her thirty-one years of work sit on shelves "holding, quietly, unsigned," and she says "I can think of no better way to be remembered than not to be." It's ironic, since a farewell is usually about being remembered, but it makes her an example of her own argument; her authority comes from not wanting credit. Then instead of an emotional finish she says "Go back to your benches. The paste is drying." The speech refuses to linger or show off, exactly like the work it praises. She is handing the shop to people who will outlast her, and the last thing she gives them isn't a memorable line but a job to finish.

s-fg2-high-1.essay:
Ottilie Brandvold's apprentices are young, and like most young craftsmen they probably judge a binding by the gold on the spine, since that is what the customer pays for and praises. Brandvold can't just tell them they are wrong, because they would hear an old woman defending slowness. So first she says their doubt out loud, and then she answers it with a story, the Alder hymnal, that shows what careful invisible work actually does for a person. By the end she has redefined patience and repair as forms of respect, and she does it in a speech that works the way she wants them to work: quiet, unsigned, and ending at the bench instead of on a big finish.

She starts by lowering the stakes of her own words. "You will not remember most of what I say this afternoon," she admits, and then explains that what she remembers of her own teacher is "his hands." For this audience that is a smart move. Apprentices who are tired of being lectured are told the lecture doesn't matter. What matters is "what you do with them when nobody is watching." From the first paragraph, value moves from what is seen to what is not. The ten-hours figure makes this concrete. If only one hour "produces something a reader can see," then an apprentice who measures by appearance is measuring a tenth of the job. Her list, "the sewing, the paring of leather to the thickness of a petal, the pressing, the waiting," slows down as it goes, and then she adds "Especially the waiting," as if she is making them wait too. The warning that a hinge "will split in the hands of a stranger three years from now" gives the hidden work a consequence they can picture. Then the sentences shrink: "Nobody will thank you for the nine hours. Do them anyway." After all that detail, the bluntness sounds like an order from a master, not a plea.

The third paragraph is where she is most persuasive, because she states the apprentices' objection for them: "Patience is a pretty word old people use to excuse slowness." She even partly agrees, calling one kind of patience "fear wearing an apron." The image is a little funny and a little insulting, and that is the point, since no apprentice wants to be the dithering binder. By giving up bad patience, she makes her own version sharper. It is "not the absence of hurry. It is the refusal of it." Now patience is something you do with force, which is easier for a young person to respect.

But a definition alone would not convince them, so she follows it with the hymnal. Mrs. Alder asks her "not to make it look new," and Brandvold spends eleven days lifting tape "a fiber at a time" while leaving the stain, "because that stain was the child." The story ends on two short fragments: "Not because I had failed to hide it. Because I had not tried." What the anecdote really does is change the question. The apprentices think the issue is speed, but the story shows the issue is what repair is for. Eleven days isn't slow if the goal is keeping a family inside a book. The next paragraph turns the story into a rule, "Repair says: this was broken, and it is still itself," and "Any factory can replace" flatters them, because only a person (only they) can repair.

The ending is where the speech practices what it preaches. Her work sits on shelves "holding, quietly, unsigned," and she can think of "no better way to be remembered than not to be." This is ironic, since she is asking the people in front of her to remember her, but she wants to live on through their hands, the way her teacher lives on in hers. Handing the bone folder to Teodor makes the farewell a handoff, not just a goodbye. And then, instead of a grand last line, she says "The paste is drying." She stops talking and sends them back to the invisible work, which is the best proof that she meant every word.

annotations.comment: Commentary on the 'fear wearing an apron' metaphor explains why it works on young apprentices (their pride), not just that it is vivid.

annotations.comment: Connects the repair/replacement definition back to the audience and explains the flattery, keeping the line of reasoning centered on the apprentices.

annotations.comment: Complex reading: the anecdote turns the apprentices' objection (patience is slowness) into a question about what repair is for. This is one of the insights the rubric names as sophistication.

annotations.comment: Places the speech in its occasion: a farewell that passes values on to people who will outlast the speaker. Paired with the irony of being remembered by not being remembered, this adds to the sophistication.

s-fg2-mid-0.essay:
In her farewell address, Ottilie Brandvold tries to convince the apprentices that the slow, hidden parts of bookbinding matter more than the parts customers can see. She does this by using concrete numbers and a personal story, so that patience stops seeming like a waste of time and starts seeming like a way of respecting the book and the people who own it.

Brandvold begins by speaking directly to the apprentices and contrasting words with hands. She says she does not expect them to remember her speech, only "your hands, and what you do with them when nobody is watching." This is a smart way to start because it shows she is not going to lecture them for a long time, and it connects to the idea of work nobody sees. She also mentions her own trainer, which makes her seem like someone who was once in their position, so the apprentices are more likely to trust her.

Next she uses a statistic to make her point more logical. She says that "of every ten hours this shop spends on a book, perhaps one produces something a reader can see." The apprentices care about what customers see, so by telling them that is only one hour she is showing them that their view is mistaken. She lists the sewing, the paring of leather, the pressing and the waiting. The list makes the hidden work feel like a lot, and then she says "Nobody will thank you for the nine hours. Do them anyway." The short sentences at the end sound like an order, and they make the point stick.

Brandvold also sees that the apprentices might disagree. In paragraph three she admits that "patience is a pretty word old people use to excuse slowness" and says some patience is "fear wearing an apron." By agreeing with them a little, she seems fair, and then she can define her own kind of patience as "the refusal of" hurry. This makes her argument stronger because she has already answered the objection.

The most powerful choice is the story of Mrs. Alder's hymnal. Brandvold spent eleven days on it and left the stain from the child's tape, and Mrs. Alder cried because Brandvold "had not tried" to hide it. This appeals to emotion and shows the apprentices that careful repair is not about looking perfect. It leads into her definition that "Repair is not replacement," which says repair keeps a book's history. After the story, the apprentices can see that slow work has a purpose.

In the end, Brandvold says she wants to be remembered by "not to be," and she tells them to go back to their benches because "The paste is drying." The ending is quiet and short, which fits what she has been saying about unshowy work. Overall, Brandvold uses logic, a concession, and a moving story to persuade the apprentices that unseen work is worth doing.

s-fg2-mid-1.essay:
In her farewell address, Ottilie Brandvold uses personal stories, hard numbers, and a emotional anecdote to convince her apprentices that the slow, hidden parts of bookbinding matter more than the parts customers see. Through these choices she shows the apprentices that patient work is not wasted time but a way of respecting the books and the people who own them.

Brandvold begins by talking about hands instead of words. She says she has forgotten the speech her own teacher gave, but she remembers that he could lift a torn signature "the way you would lift a sleeping child from a chair." This comparison makes careful work seem gentle and loving, and it also gives her credibility because she was once an apprentice just like them, with "glue on my cuffs." The apprentices are likely to listen to someone who admits she stood in their shoes. By asking them to remember their hands "when nobody is watching," she introduces the idea of unseen work right away.

Next she uses a statistic to make her point more logical. She says that of every ten hours spent on a book, only one produces "something a reader can see." The gold on the spine and the marbled endpapers are that one hour, while the other nine are sewing, paring leather, and waiting. This matters to apprentices who judge their work by what customers notice, because it shows them that most of the job is something customers never see. She then warns that a hinge glued too soon will split "in the hands of a stranger three years from now," which shows the bad results of rushing. Her short command "Do them anyway" is a big drop in sentence length and sounds firm.

The strongest part of the speech is the story of Mrs. Alder's hymnal. Brandvold spent eleven days on it and left the stain beneath the kitchen tape, because "that stain was the child." When Mrs. Alder wept, it was "because I had not tried" to hide it. This story is emotional, and it proves that repair means keeping history instead of erasing it. After this she defines repair against replacement, saying "Any factory can replace. Only a person can repair." This makes the apprentices feel their slow work is something a machine cannot do, which makes it worth doing.

Finally, the ending turns personal. Brandvold says her work sits "unsigned" on shelves in houses she has never entered, and that she wants to be remembered by not being remembered. Her last line, "The paste is drying," is short and sends them back to work. Overall, Brandvold persuades her apprentices by mixing emotion, logic, and her own experience so that invisible work feels important and honorable.

s-fg2-low-0.essay:
In her farewell address Ottilie Brandvold uses many rhetorical choices to persuade the apprentices. She uses ethos, pathos and logos to get her audience to value the careful work of bookbinding even when no one sees it.

First, Brandvold starts by talking directly to the apprentices. She says "You will not remember most of what I say this afternoon" and then talks about the man who trained her and his hands. This makes her seem like she is humble and also like she was once in their shoes. She says she will ask them to remember their hands instead of her words. This is a good way to start a speech because it gets the audience's attention.

Next she uses statistics. She says that out of ten hours only one produces something a reader can see. This is logos because it uses a number to prove her point. She lists the gold on the spine and the marbled endpapers and then says the other nine hours go into sewing and pressing and waiting. This shows the audience that most of the work is not seen. Then she says "Do them anyway" which is short and strong.

Brandvold also tells a story about Mrs. Alder and the hymnal. This is pathos because Mrs. Alder cried when she saw the book. The story shows that repair is important and it makes the audience feel emotional. It also shows that Brandvold is good at her job so she has credibility.

In the end she says "The paste is drying" which tells them to go back to work. Overall, Brandvold uses these choices to persuade the apprentices and she does it well by using ethos, pathos and logos and by showing that patient work matters.

annotations.comment: Labels the device and asserts it proves something, without explaining how the one-in-ten ratio challenges the apprentices' habit of measuring work by visible results. The evidence is accurate but the commentary is only a label.
